title: The Snares
body:
Tomas is ten years old. He has no mother and no father. He lives in a monastery in the mountains, the monastery of Saint Ansel. Many monks live there, and twelve children live there too. The children are all orphans, like Tomas.

Tomas has two friends. Bram is eleven. He is the oldest boy in the monastery. He is tall and loud, and he likes to tell the other children what to do. Pip is eight. He is small and funny, and he talks all day. He talks to birds, to trees and to animals.

Tomas is different. He is quiet. He does not talk much, but he looks at everything and he thinks a lot.

In spring the food in the monastery is not good. Every day there is only bread and a little soup. The boys are always hungry.

Early in the morning, before the monks get up, the three boys climb over the wall and go into the forest. This is not allowed. The abbot, Father Gerard, says it every week: “No children in the forest!” But the boys want meat.

In the forest the boys have snares. A snare is a small trap for rabbits. Tomas makes very good snares.

“Be quiet!” says Bram. But Bram is the loudest of the three.

The first snare is empty. Tomas sees some grey hair on the rope. “There was a rabbit here,” he says. “But it is gone.”

“Your snare is bad,” says Bram.

Tomas does not answer. His snare is not bad. He makes the knot stronger and puts the snare a little lower.

In the second snare there is a rabbit. Bram takes it, and he is very happy. “I have a rabbit!” he says. But it is Tomas's snare, not Bram's.

On the way home, Pip stops. On an old tree there is a grey rabbit with a torn ear. It looks at the boys. It is not afraid.

“Look! That is the rabbit from the first snare,” says Pip. “He is very clever. His name is the King.”

Near an old path, Tomas stops again. On the ground he sees the marks of horses. They are big and new. Who has big horses here? Only rich men. Tomas looks at the marks for a long time, but he says nothing to Bram and Pip.

Brother Anselm is at the gate of the monastery. He is an old monk, very kind. He knows where the boys were.

The boys must copy a page from an old book. It is the story of an emperor. “His blood came down from the stars,” says the book.

“It is only a story,” says Bram.

Brother Anselm smiles. “Many things are only stories,” he says. “Until one day they are not.”

title: Thieves in the Night
body:
It is night. Everybody in the monastery is asleep. Only Tomas is awake. He thinks about the horse marks in the forest. Who comes to a monastery on big horses? Maybe men who want to come back at night, he thinks.

Then he hears a noise outside. He goes to the window. The moon is big and bright. In the yard there are four men. They go to the chapel. In the chapel the monks have two beautiful things: an old silver cup and a small gold box. These things are very old and very expensive.

“Thieves!” thinks Tomas.

The monks are good men, but they cannot fight. And Tomas cannot fight four men. If he shouts, the thieves run away with the silver. He needs a plan.

He wakes Bram. “Bram, listen,” he says quietly. “Go up the bell tower. When I knock on the wall two times, ring the bell. Ring it very loud!”

Bram wants to say something. He does not like it when Tomas tells him what to do. But he looks at Tomas's face, and he goes.

Pip wakes up too. He sees the men in the yard and he is very afraid. He hides under a bench, and he stays there all night.

Tomas takes his rope for the snares and runs down the stairs to the cellar. The cellar has a door to the forest. The thieves want to go out this way, he thinks. On the third stair he ties the rope from one wall to the other. It is low and tight, like a snare for rabbits.

Then he knocks on the wall. One, two.

The bell rings. It is very, very loud. The monks wake up, and there are lights in all the windows. The thieves are afraid. They run to the cellar with the silver. The first thief does not see the rope. He falls down the stairs and he cries out. His leg is broken. The other thieves drop the cup and the box, and they run into the forest.

Tomas goes back up to the window. Near the trees he sees a fifth man. The man does not run. He is not with the thieves. He only looks at the windows of the children's bedroom. He has only one eye. Is he counting the children?

In the morning, everybody talks about the night. “The bell is my idea,” says Bram, and the monks say Bram is a hero. Tomas says nothing. For him that is OK.

But he does not tell anybody about the man with one eye.

title: Counting Heads
body:
After the night of the thieves, the monastery is quiet again. The lord's men come and take the thief with the broken leg to the castle. “Now everything is OK,” they say. The abbot is happy. “God looks after our home,” he says, and he says thank you to Bram for the bell.

One week later, a man comes to the monastery. He buys and sells wool. He has two big wagons, four horses and a servant. He is very nice. He has good clothes and he speaks politely. He buys the wool of the monastery for a good price, and he gives the monks a big barrel of wine.

The man has only one eye. On the other eye he has a black patch.

Tomas sees him, and he knows: that is the man from the night.

The trader wants to leave the next day, but he does not leave. One day his wagon has a broken wheel. The next day it rains. Tomas sees that the man is always near the children. He asks the young monks a lot of questions. “How many children live here? How old are they? Do they go to the forest alone?”

Tomas goes to the abbot. “Father, that man was here on the night of the thieves,” he says. “I saw him near the forest.”

The abbot looks at him. He is kind, but he does not believe Tomas. “It was night, Tomas, and it was dark. Now you see a man with one eye, and you think: that is the man. No. We do not judge a man by his face.”

Bram laughs at Tomas. “You want to be a hero, like me,” he says.

Pip has a new friend: the trader. Every afternoon the man gives Pip a honey cake, and Pip goes everywhere with him, like a little dog. “He is very nice,” says Pip. “He asks me about our snares in the forest, so I show him where they are.”

On the third day the trader leaves. He smiles and waves from his wagon. In the evening nobody talks about him, and soon everybody forgets him.

But Tomas does not forget. At night he goes to the kitchen. He takes a small knife and a long rope for snares. He puts the knife and the rope under his shirt. From this day he always has them with him. Every day. Every night.
